title_original: In Every Dream Home a Heartache: James Gray on Paper Tiger

blocks.text: With every James Gray movie, a new chance for James Gray to become a household name. (Almost no filmmaker will ever achieve that status again, but just follow me here.) Paper Tiger is perhaps the best-yet synthesis of his great instincts with commercial viability, and—because these things never exist in a vacuum—one of 2026’s few films to cross over the “movie for adults” and “can recommend to anyone” Venn diagram. This, and no dissolving or short-changing Gray’s feel for character and place, nor his movie-star triumvirate failing to explicate the material. Were there but five more films with such traits produced and released at a similar scale, cinephiles’ sky-is-falling routine would have much less weight. Right now, we just hope it creates suitable runway for its auteur’s next project.

Gray’s actors are so famous as to not walk down the street safely; he remains a working filmmaker. Thus our conversation was delayed by his shooting a commercial in upstate New York, and by the time we caught up he was in a Paris hotel room for other assignments, speaking via Zoom.
James Gray: Hi, Nick. How are you?
The Film Stage: I’m well. I believe you’re in Paris?
I am indeed. Massively jetlagged. I kind of don’t know which way is up, but it’s a high-class problem, I like to say. Better that they want to talk to you and see you than they don’t, right?
I would say so. Were you shooting a commercial?

Well, that was a two-day shoot. I had to pay my bills, because you’re not working through this whole stretch that you’re promoting a movie, and I’ve been flying all over with the movie [Laughs] and just squeezed in these two days of work to shoot in upstate New York. The hours were just crazy because they had to do it in two days because of me, as opposed to three or four, and so it’s been a lot.
Where upstate?

Well, I shouldn’t say “upstate”—that’s a bit of an exaggeration—but it’s about an hour-and-a-half outside the zone, in Rockland County. “Upstate” from me. I don’t mean Troy or Buffalo. It’s beautiful, by the way—it’s one of the most beautiful parts of the world, up that Palisades Highway drive. You can see how it inspired all those great artists. You can see Frederic Church painting these amazing works of art based on the beauty of the Hudson. It’s really quite magnificent, and sort of an underrated part of the country.

It’s not the East River School for a reason. Anyway, you did this terrific interview with Filmmaker Magazine that focused a lot on the sound. One question I had while watching the movie that I don’t think went answered there is sound’s relation to time—elements of the soundscape that have to be distinct to this era. Car sounds are an obvious one. But in a melange of street traffic, could you technically record something outside my window right now and pass it off as 1986? Maybe something has to be there to evoke the era.

[Shakes head] The electric-car sound—the whine of the electric car is just completely wrong. You’re talking about a very analogue world. The idea, also, was not just the analogue, industrial world—or what was beginning to be the post-industrial world, the beginning—but also the natural world infringing upon it at times. You have the sounds of the city, but also the ending, with Adam Driver, the whole intention was that he returns to the natural world: he leaves the city behind him, in a metaphoric sense. So you have to have both. You know, life is both: life is the assault of the city, but even in the assault you can still hear birds sometimes. You’re trying to get a balanced kind of idea.

I don’t really restrict my idea of sound to one thing or other. It’s not literal, it’s not abstract—it’s both. The influences can be David Lynch and Polanski; Friedkin is another big one with sound. Obviously Walter Murch’s work is incredibly important. In his case, he used a lot of practical or justified sounds, but in weird places: the train roar under Al Pacino’s stern face before he kills Al Lettieri and Sterling Hayden, or the strange sounds of foghorns that he puts all over The Conversation , or the train-crossing sounds he puts all over The Conversation . So there’s no rules with sound. You can use literal sound in the wrong place, literal sound in the right place, surreal sound in what should be a very quotidian scene. I mean, that’s the real weapon that you have; it’s the way that you can access the unconscious.

Now, when the visuals don’t justify it at all, it can decouple from the style of the film. So you do have to think about sound design while you’re making the movie—you know, the mood of the scene—but the analogue world is very different from what we have now. The overwhelming sound of cell phone alarms and the whine of electric cars. Even the sirens of police and ambulances sound different. So you can’t just go out and record the sound of the street and say that’s 1986. You simply can’t. In the same way that if you were to make a film in 1980 about 1940, you’d have to have the “a-WOO-ga” on your soundtrack, and that was gone by 1950. It’s an ever-shifting universe, and as time passes, the places and things that we attach ourselves to, in some way or another in our memory, are but thin slices of time in the landscape.

The house in this film was compelling to me, because at some points you see the street and all of these houses in a long line look the same. Of course there’s the old notion about eight-million stories in the naked city, and this one house in an identical procession made me wonder why you chose that particular exterior at that particular point on the street, and how you make a decision like that.

You know, a lot of that is instinctual. It’s a wonderful question. You’re using some aspect of your memory combined with an idea—not necessarily of what’s real, but what feels authentic—and that’s somewhat instinctual. But also the color of the house. Some houses are garish, and if you shoot them on film, they look ostentatious in a way you don’t want to imply about the character. So it sends you the wrong message. You know: the characters who buy a house that was brick and not aluminum siding. Why? Because he would be an engineer and he would know aluminum siding looks not-great after the first year, and the brick stands up better—all of that.

So I just think that the governing principles are character, context, and really a kind of sense of instinctual aesthetics. And of course you’re very right about the row-house thing, which I haven’t articulated before, so you’re [Laughs] the first person ever to ask me about it. But the whole idea is that in every house there is a story worth telling. There is great drama. My life is not the only life which has had tremendous drama. Yours has. Everybody’s has. The question is: are you unflinching in your approach to it? Most people are not. It’s very uncomfortable to shoot, almost literally, a fight between your mother and father where your mother hits your father and he doesn’t hit back. It’s uncomfortable. And people are going to, “Uck. Ick. I don’t want to see that. It’s uncomfortable. It’s terrible.” But the truth is: that happens in every house in one way or another. Whose life is free from tragedy? So you’re just saying that this house is one of eight-billion stories on that block.
“In Every Dream Home a Heartache” is a line that resonates with me a lot.

Exactly. And it’s our job to dramatize that. Because if you deny that—if you spend your time saying, “This is a particular story that wouldn’t happen anywhere else”—you’re actually invalidating everybody’s story. Every time somebody experiences something like that, they’re weird. It’s unusual. One of the things you realize is that that’s, no, actually quite common. So I’m not saying everybody has run-ins with the Russian organizatsiya trying to extort your parents. That’s a matter of fact ; that’s a matter of degree. It’s not really a matter of emotion. Everybody goes through traumatic stuff. How do we know this? Because we are all mortal.
I’ve heard you mention in a couple of interviews over the years the experience of seeing someone get shot on Saint Marks Place.
That’s right. Coming out of a record store called Sounds. Horrible.
I would say that left a mark on you—how could it not—but is that something you’ve carried into your work and representations of violence?

I would never say it didn’t affect me. Maybe what I’m saying—you forget these things because I’m doing a lot of talking and I’m sure I sound stupid in 98% of it—was distinguishing that, something I witnessed, from something that was visited directly upon me. It did hugely. First of all, let me be clear about this: I didn’t see somebody get shot, because I didn’t actually see the shooting. I heard it , and then turned to look . I saw the immediate aftermath. I wasn’t watching somebody get shot. Obviously I heard it, turned, there was somebody on the street, he had the horrible moaning sound. You realize that, you know, the only thing that keeps order is the most thin layer of, actually, implied violence: if you do X, we’ll do Y to you. That’s how order is maintained. And it’s a thin layer.

You know, what the Rodney King riots taught us was that the second the top blew at all, the cops stood back and it was total disorder. Total disorder. The 1977 blackouts in New York was a very big deal to me because that was also—on the drive home from Herman’s Sporting Goods, I remember—the lights illuminating the streets, seeing people running back and forth, taking stuff from stores. It really gave me a sense, I think, of how tenuous the idea of order actually is, and how you achieve order, and how order is really maintained only through a certain kind of violence. That is a powerful and very upsetting notion: that if you, for example, didn’t have a police force at all, what would happen? Well, what would happen very quickly is that we would devolve into chaos. That is a haunting notion, to know how thin that line is.

There’s a classic “gangster movie” moment here where Adam Driver whips the guys in takeout place. I have to confess that you got me riled up—I hated these Russian thugs terrorizing this poor family so much that I felt satisfaction and catharsis.

Absolutely. You should. That’s absolutely true. Part of what has really screwed up art, if I may say, is the idea that you have to take a morally correct stance at all times. In other words: the creative person is teaching you Sunday school. That’s not really what our function is. You’re meant to enjoy that to some degree, because that’s the darker side of us and that’s in us, and the work of art cannot avoid speaking of our worst impulses. You know, this idea that we’re supposed to advertise an only morally and ethically correct idea—that violence is always repugnant—this is not true. Sometimes human beings take pleasure in violence. That’s part of the complexity of our story. That’s why [hums “Ride of the Valkyries”] in Apocalypse is so great: you are engaged in a pleasure, but it’s ugly, but it’s us. It’s in us. The film invites you to take a pleasure in that, and then to say that that pleasure is only part of the story. Now, if the movie is only about the pleasure of violence, you have a piece of junk. But if the film includes the pleasure of violence that we sometimes feel, and the harm of it, that’s the whole picture. If there was no pleasure in violence, nobody would ever go hunting. People hunt. Why do they hunt? They find pleasure in the kill. That’s who we are.

But also: you asked me before about the presentation of violence. My idea was never to glorify, and this film was only to imply it in many places because the idea is that it was so big, so vast, so omnipresent that to depict it in its microcosm would be impossible. So the violence sits outside the frame. Offscreen place. Shadows implying something. Trying to see the killer through the weeds but you can’t. You hear them but you don’t see them. They approach the car, the window is fogged. The idea is that the violence is bigger than we can really get a handle on. Bigger than we know.
Photo by Mettie Ostrowski, courtesy of the 64th New York Film Festival.
Part of what I mean about it being a classic “gangster movie” moment is that there’s the hack version of it, which is intense close-ups while a ‘50s pop song plays. A bad Goodfellas riff.
[Laughs]
And the austerity of it. Do you recall the thinking that went into the framing?

I sure do. What I was trying to say is that this sort of thing happens every day, and you could be walking past the glass and see it. And that I didn’t want you to take pleasure in the violence, but I wanted you to know that that pleasure exists. It’s a very fine line. So: to get in there and engage. You know, one of the reasons that maestro Scorsese gets away with it—in Goodfellas in particular—is that the film is actually a comedy. And it was a really brilliant decision that Marty made, to pitch it in a way—it’s a very subversive idea—that you would enjoy the violence so much and understand it as, really, an outgrowth of capitalism. A perverse outgrowth, but an outgrowth. This movie’s not a comedy, so you can’t do it. In Raging Bull , the idea of the violence is that it’s so connected, inextricably, with his destruction. He’s letting it get done to himself so he gets away with it there.

But this is a different kind of story. I mean, this is a story where this family that doesn’t really acknowledge or live in the darkness at the beginning is forced to see that it’s there. So I treated the violence in a very different way—almost eyewitness—so that you could be walking past the store and see it. When you get into it and you get close on it, it’s an idea of fetish out of the context of the rest of the story and what I set up.
This movie puts as much weight into a slap as it does a gunshot. Irwin getting slapped is quite upsetting. It’s no joke.

Yeah, no, not at all. I’m going to be pretentious here for a second, but that comes from when Prince Myshkin is slapped in The Idiot . It’s a humiliation to it, an emasculation. It’s not only an act of violence. It’s an act of violence both meant to intimidate and humiliate . Humiliation is the single most potent force and motive for anguish. If you ever read—not that you should, necessarily—about Mohamed Atta, who was one of the more important 9/11 hijackers, he was not from a poor family; he was from a middle-class family in Egypt. His father was a doctor. So what happened to him? Well, the answer to what happened to him was: he was routinely humiliated in Germany and he couldn’t tolerate it. Humiliation was his motive, not deprivation. So when we talk about these things, that slap is meant as a weapon beyond threat. It’s a tool to say “you are small, not vast.” So that’s why I think it has the weight that it does.
I also appreciate the “pretension” of raising Dostoevsky. That’s totally acceptable.

No, I mean, we live in a country—much as I love the United States, and I do; I really love it; I’m an American through and through—but we have a real anti-intellectual streak. We seem to think that people who have read books are losers or dorks or nerds or idiots. It’s always been the case, and I think it’s, among our many great qualities, maybe one of our worst. And it’s not the whole country, it’s not everybody, but there is especially now, with these online people, those who resent the high-falutin reference. So I always feel now the need to apologize for it, but you’re quite right: we shouldn’t. We shouldn’t.
I know you’re a great admirer of Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me .
Oh, it’s a masterpiece.
Did you ever see the third season? What did you think of it?

The third season of Twin Peaks ? I thought that it was magnificent in some cases and sort of uneven. Stuff that was incredible and always worth watching, by the way— always worth watching—but stuff that was absolutely amazing and stuff that was self-conscious. But of course worth watching because I love him. The other thing I would say is: I prefer David’s work when he was a little more narratively based. I don’t need a ton of narrative—it’s a personal issue—and I also liked when his work evinced great sympathy for the protagonist. I’m a little bit old-school in that way. When he made Wild at Heart , it’s one of my lesser-favorite Lynches, because it seems to almost be tackily making fun of everybody.
I agree.

But Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me , I saw that in an empty movie theater with two friends of mine. I was prepared to hate it because of everything that I had read about it—boos in Cannes and everyone I knew hated the movie—and I just couldn’t believe how misunderstood it was. It was one of the most compassionate, beautiful films I’d seen, and it really remains one of the happiest moments I’ve ever had in a movie theater. I’ve seen films I loved in theaters all the time , but I’d never seen one that I so anticipated thinking would stink , so friggin’ great . That same year, I saw two other films, I remember, that I loved. One was Unforgiven . I had weirdly high expectations of Unforgiven , and I wound up loving the film, but I didn’t expect to hate it, you know? I expected to like it. Maybe because I liked some of his other pictures a lot. But this was a real shock to the system.

I want to say that I have many flaws as a person, obviously—I’m certainly limited in many ways—but I was right about that movie. And I was way ahead of the curve on it [Laughs] if I can brag. I said so as soon as I saw it. I told David Lynch; I told his then-significant other and -editor Mary Sweeney after seeing it. I met David Lynch. He was the head of the jury at the Venice Film Festival when I took Little Odessa there, and he was instrumental in supporting that film, so I had a lovely connection with David Lynch. But that film, it really does speak to compassion for [Laura Palmer] in a way that is sui generis and a thing of beauty.
And I would say the exact same about your films.

Oh, thank you. That’s very sweet. And that’s the ambition. What I have found—and look, I don’t know if I succeed—but what I have found is that that kind of thing, it actually initially doesn’t always catch fire. Not always initially. It’s a Wonderful Life , for example. Vertigo . These kind of pictures. But they wear very well over time. What happens is that people seem to connect with it—not expecting something else from it after a while—it begins to reveal itself as filled with compassion and with love. And if that’s your ambition, I think you’re always gonna be okay.
We’re out of time. I appreciate you taking a moment from this jetlagged trip.
Bye, Nick. Thanks for your support over the years. I really appreciate it. I do.
Paper Tiger is now in theaters.
